doc.title: Benny Waters interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

title: Being a living historian; Europe made up for the States
summary: He says Europe's reception made up for what he did not earn in the States, and recalls playing organ concerts as a three-year-old boy wonder.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You know you are a living historian. Every time you play, you know, you’re the oldest internationally touring musician active in jazz. So every time you play, you are history. What does that feel like?

Well I don’t know. That’s what people say, you know they say, not mine. I’m just doing the best I can you know, see? I’m not — how the people feel, their reaction it’s up to the people you know? I haven’t been playing so much in the States, but in Europe, the reaction has been great, you know. Stand up ovations and so forth, every place I play. Crowded places, you know? And I was telling some friend of mine, I said jazz don’t owe me anything because what I didn’t make financially in the States, I made up for it in Europe. See so it’s been good to me you know?
That’s a wonderful story too. The fact that you have this positive relationship with the art form itself.

Yes well I’ve been in it a long time, see? I was playing as a soloist organ in the church and in concerts when I was three years old. I had my sister pumping the thing. I forget the name of that organ in that little church, the country organ. I couldn’t reach the pedals, you know, you play like that. I couldn’t reach it. I was too short. And my sister used to pump while I’d play. And I was doing concerts. It was booked as a boy wonder you know, one of those things. So I’ve been playing as a soloist a long time.
